chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Rock and roll's roots in the thirties and rhythm and blues
summary: Horace says rocking and swinging existed long before rock and roll, citing Clara and Bessie Smith and 'Good Rockin' Tonight', admired by Hammond.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: A moment ago you used the term, rocking out. You said the man was really rocking out. Do you have any idea, could you recall when you first heard or when that term was applied to music, because it really was applied long before the term, rock and roll. And I'm just wondering if you might have any idea about that.
You mean -- speaking of swing, right?

You know, I dwell a lot on the '30's, Tom, because a lot of things happened in those days, like a lot of people have thought that rock and roll is something new or had been something new, but a lot of those things were played back in those days. It just didn't have the name rock and roll.
Yeah. That's true. Well, there's no question that rock and roll grew directly out of rhythm and blues.

Why sure. And, you know how important rhythm and blues was in those days. If you don't think so, let's check with John Hammond and he can enlighten you plenty, because that's a guy that, in the days that, since we're talking about rhythm and blues, there were two great blues singers way back in that era that John Hammond idolized, you know. They were Clara and Bessie Smith. No relation -- but, man, could they sing the blues. I mean they sang from here -- to your heart, you know. And they could really belt out things like that.
They did things that singers are just doing today, you know.

Yeah, that's true. Well, you can listen to a lot of the old recordings and just see where all of that came from. Well, there was a drummer, Roy Brown? I'm not sure. He's still around today too. Maybe I'm using the wrong name, but back in the late '40's he wrote a song, and the titled -- used the word rocking in it. And in fact -- I may be wrong again -- 'There's Good Rockin' Tonight' or something like that.
Yeah, yeah. Yeah, way back then.
And I was just wondering if, you
know, you could recall hearing or using that term prior to that time.

That particular tune I remember, There's Good Rocking Tonight, you know, and it was used by a lot of good blues singers in those days that actually they didn't become known as well as, you know, certain blues singers that have come up. But I just happened to think, you know, way back -- we're talking about then. One of the greatest blues singers, as far as I'm concerned, in those days was Joe Turner, out of Kansas City.
